questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I chose to go abroad both for academic opportunities and to explore new cultures. 
I wanted to stay within Europe and go to an English-speaking country for it to be easier to interact with local people and take part in local social life. Furthermore Ireland I believe that Ireland has a lively and significant culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I got to experience other cultures and try out new and different courses which was great. Also exploring Ireland was great. I had hoped that cork would be a more historically beautiful city and I had a tough time missing friends and family.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: You can always contact the international office with questions either in person or by email. In general information about courses and so is given very late in Ireland, so be patient. I chose my courses very late and I couldn't access the timetables prior to this. Be sure to have looked at plenty of interesting courses at UCC before you apply to as you only very late will see which might overlap.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Again the international office was open and there were also several welcome meetings for all international students. The international office also hosts a swap shop with items donated by the prior international students where you pay a small fee and can grab whatever you need.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Ireland is experiencing a housing crisis which makes all accommodation very expensive. UCC offers accommodation for a few students, but you won't know if you are accepted for this until very close to arrival in Cork. By then it might be difficult to find other types of accommodation. I chose to find accommodation on my own. I lived at Hatch: Marsh's Yard which is a student accommodation close to the city but about a 25-35 min walk to campus. It was nice living close to the city to explore and use the shops and areas there. It is a very new and nice accommodation, but it was also very expensive.
I know some other international students who had to buy kitchen supplies in their accommodation, but Hatch had everything ready for you to use. You share kitchen and common room with 2-5 other student but i believe everyone has their own bathroom. You can find this on their website where you also can choose differently priced rooms.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can be quite far from campus, but closer to the city. The campus is situated west of town.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You choose your courses just about a month before arrival and you don't know the timetables before this. This means that the courses you want to take potentially will overlap. Because of this you should have some “backup courses” in mind. Furthermore, the dates and deadline for this process were changed which could create confusion.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You choose your courses in a program online and you can put different courses into a timetable to see if anything overlaps.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You get a very detailed mail with a description of the process which helped a lot! You could always email the international office for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was lucky that my courses actually fit into a schedule without any overlaps. On the other hand I had several overlapping exams in the end, but you won't know about this until November so don't worry about this. Many international students have overlapping exams and there is a special procedure for this.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Stay calm and follow the detailed guide you are given. Check your mail often during this period.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very happy with some courses, but others had really unstructured professors.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I think it really depends on what courses you take. I had a course in “Developmental Genetics” in which I found out (a little too late) that I didn't really have enough prior knowledge and this made the course very tough. On the other hand, I had an “introduction to pharmacology “course where we went through some of the things I knew from KU, but we build new knowledge upon that afterward which was really nice.
For me, the course  “Introduction to “Modern Irish History for  Visiting Students” was a bit too advanced for students who don't have any prior knowledge of Irish history.
You should note that in Ireland a bachelor's degree takes 4 years and a master only 1 year. So 1xxx, 2xxx, 3xxx and 4xxx courses are bachelor leven and 5xxx is master level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching was again very different from course to course, but in general, I feel like KU is a highly structured institution compared to UCC. In “Virology” I ended up being so confused after each lecture because no lecture had a specific theme and we had no plan for the semester. On the other hand, I had great teachers in my pharmacology courses and here there was a more structured approach, which I personally thrive in.
I believe you call your professors by their last name, but I feel like the professor/student relationship is very chill, and the professors are very happy to answer questions.
My courses consisted mainly of lectures and there were no scheduled smaller classes like SAU or TØ to go through the material, which I missed from KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
HI1115: Introduction to Modern Irish History for Visiting Students 5 ECTS
MB3022: Virology 5 ECTS
PT3001: Introduction to Pharmacology 5 ECTS
PT4005: Neuropharmacology 5 ECTS
BC4011: Cell and molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease 5 ECTS
GN4001: Developmental Genetics 5 ECTS

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would really recommend Introduction to Pharmacology and Neuropharmacology which were both great courses with great professors. Both courses build upon the knowledge I had and sparked my interest in pharmacology and the development of drugs. Both courses go through specific diseases, what the problem is, and how this is (tried) solved with drugs. This made it very “reality close” and specific which I enjoyed. On the other hand, you should be prepared to practice drug names which can be tough haha.
Cell and molecular Basis of Neurodegenerative disease was also a great course about Alzheimer's and Parkinsons'. The structure of the course is a little messier, but the professor is very engaged in her research and the field which made the course great.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The accommodation was very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Accommodation is very expensive, but groceries are a little cheaper than in Denmark. 
A big gym with fitness classes is included in your enrollment at UCC which is great. Also clubs and societies are free to join.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many clubs (for sports) and societies (for interests) at UCC so there is plenty of new stuff to try out and it is possible to find a community with people who have the same interests as you. These are all free to attend. Clubs include boxing, swimming, canoeing, mountaineering, and much more. Examples of societies are the environmental society, the yoga and meditation society, the photography and film society, and the foodie society.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
It can be difficult to get a spot at one of the club training as the university is quite big and has a lot of students. This means that you sometimes have to be ready to book a spot at the training in the portal. The mountaineering club is a great way to go on hikes in the Irish landscape but they are quite tough! Wear hiking boots even though they say that trainers are okay for beginner hikes. 
You should definitely just try out different clubs and societies! It's free and if you don't enjoy it you don't have to keep going to the trainings and meetings. It's also a nice way to meet new friends.

´

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: A local group of people called Cork International Students  arrange some free actitvities and priced weekend trips for international students in Cork. I went on one of these trips to Kerry and visited the Killarney national park, which was a great experience. Getting around Ireland can be difficult as the infrastructure is quite bad, but you can go on guided day trips by bus to several locations. I went to Slea Head and Gougane Barra which were both beautiful places.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy - they are quite similar to us in many ways.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be brave and start a conversation. Ask questions. Attend clubs and societies as there are many local students here.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciated the trad music at pubs, when the locals called me “love” and hearing about the Irish history. I also got to drink the Irish Guinness and the local equivalent Beamish.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be patient in regards to information - it will come but much closer to semester start than in Denmark.
Engage in clubs and societies to meet new both international and Irish friends. It is also a great. 
Start looking for accommodation early on as it might be difficult to find later.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the possibility to try out different courses within my field of interest and some of these really sparked my interest in drug development. It was cool getting to see the wild nature of Ireland and to meet young people from all over the world and learn about their culture and how it was different from mine.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was tough for me to be away from my friends and family and I go quite homesick at times. I think you should talk to other international students about this as it is quite common.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I had the idea that this was supposed to be the travel/trip of my life which kinda puts pressure on everything to be amazing and great. You have lots of time to travel to other places later in life so don't put so much pressure on this trip. It's okay if not everything is amazing and that it sometimes can be tough.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
